stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Producing a color woodcut in nineteenth-century Japan took several specialists. Each workshop was headed by a single master printer, who answered to the publisher. After an artist finished a design, a carver cut a separate block for each color. Finally, the ______ aligned those blocks on damp paper, using small notches cut into the wood so that every color landed in exactly the right place.
explanation: The assistants belong to the printer, so "printer" needs an apostrophe. The passage says each workshop had a single master printer, so you need the singular possessive "printer's." The assistants own nothing. They are the subject of "aligned," so "assistants" is plural with no apostrophe.

B.why: You left the apostrophe off "printers." The printer owns the assistants, so the word has to be possessive, and "printers" with no apostrophe is only a plural.

C.why: You marked the right noun as the owner but made it plural. The passage says each workshop was headed by a single master printer, so "printers'" names more owners than the text describes.

D.why: You put an apostrophe on "assistants," but the assistants don't own anything. The word comes right before the verb "aligned" and is only plural.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Self-reported diet records are notoriously unreliable, so a team of nutrition researchers tried a different approach. Over twelve weeks, they asked 240 volunteers to photograph every meal before eating it. The ______ revealed that most people underestimated their portion sizes by nearly a third, especially for snacks eaten late in the evening.
explanation: The photographs belong to the volunteers, and the passage says there were 240 of them. A plural owner that ends in s takes the apostrophe after the s, so "volunteers'." The photographs own nothing. They are the subject of "revealed," so "photographs" is a plain plural.

A.why: You made the owner possessive but singular. The passage names 240 volunteers, so the photographs belong to more than one person, and you need "volunteers'."

B.why: You put the apostrophe on the wrong noun. "Photographs" comes right before the verb "revealed" and owns nothing, while "volunteers," the real owner, has no apostrophe.

D.why: You gave the apostrophe to "photograph," which owns nothing, and left the real owner, "volunteers," without one. The verb "revealed" also needs a plural subject, not a possessive.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Sprint coaches have long disagreed about how much rest athletes need between all-out efforts. To test the question, physiologist Lena Osei timed a group of eighteen collegiate sprinters over repeated 60-meter dashes. She recorded the ______ after rest periods of one, three, and five minutes and found that performance barely recovered until the three-minute mark.
explanation: The speeds belong to the sprinters, and the passage says there were eighteen of them. That means a plural possessive: "sprinters'." The speeds themselves own nothing. They are only the object of "recorded," so "speeds" takes no apostrophe.

A.why: You put the apostrophe on "speeds," which owns nothing, and left the real owner, "sprinters," without one.

B.why: You found the right owner but made it singular. The passage describes eighteen sprinters, so "sprinter's" names one owner when there are several.

D.why: You made "speed" possessive even though it owns nothing, and you left "sprinters" without the apostrophe it needs to show ownership.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Most plant fossils survive only as flattened smudges of carbon, but one specimen recovered from an Illinois coal seam is unusually complete. explanation: The leaves belong to the fossil, and the passage describes only one specimen, so you need the singular possessive "specimen's." The leaves own nothing. They are the subject of "show," so "leaves" takes no apostrophe.

A.why: You left the apostrophe off the owner. The leaves belong to the specimen, so "specimen" has to be possessive. "Specimens" is only a plural.

C.why: You made the owner plural, but the passage is about one specimen from a single coal seam. One owner takes 's.

D.why: You got "specimen's" right but also added an apostrophe to "leaves." That noun comes right before the verb "show" and owns nothing.

C.why: You got "network's" right but also put an apostrophe on "computer's." That noun owns nothing and comes right before the verb "compare," so it needs to be the plain plural "computers."

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Cliff swallows build their nests from hundreds of small mud pellets, and a colony may contain several hundred pairs crowded beneath a single bridge or rock overhang. This arrangement offers protection from predators, but it has a cost. Because the ______ are packed so tightly together, parasites such as the swallow bug can spread quickly through an entire colony in a single season.
explanation: The nests belong to the birds, and the passage describes several hundred pairs, so you need the plural possessive "birds'." The nests own nothing. They are the subject of "are packed," so "nests" takes no apostrophe.

A.why: You left the apostrophe off "birds." The nests belong to the birds, so the word has to be possessive, not just plural.

B.why: You made the owner singular even though the colony holds hundreds of birds. You also added an apostrophe to "nests," which comes right before the verb and owns nothing.

D.why: You moved the apostrophe to "nest's," which owns nothing, and left the real owner, "birds," without one. The plural verb "are" also needs the plural "nests."

stimulus: In the 1890s, Norwegian cartographer Ingrid Halvorsen spent three summers charting the narrow fjords north of Bergen. explanation: The measurements belong to Halvorsen, who is one person, so the owner takes 's: "Halvorsen's." The measurements own nothing. They are the subject of "were," so "measurements" is a plain plural.

A.why: You left the apostrophe off the owner. The measurements belong to Halvorsen, so her name has to be possessive.

C.why: You put the apostrophe after an s, which signals several owners named Halvorsen. The passage says she worked mostly alone, so there is only one owner.

D.why: You got "Halvorsen's" right but also added an apostrophe to "measurement's." That noun owns nothing and comes right before the plural verb "were."

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: By the 1780s, the silk industry of Lyon, France, employed many thousands of weavers, most of whom worked for merchants rather than for themselves. Few large factories existed. Instead, most of the ______ were set up in the workers' own homes, where spouses and children helped wind thread and tie the cords that controlled each pattern.
explanation: The looms belong to the weavers, and the passage describes many thousands of them, so you need the plural possessive "weavers'." The looms own nothing. They are the subject of "were set up," so "looms" takes no apostrophe.

A.why: You left the apostrophe off "weavers." The looms belong to the weavers, so the word has to be possessive, not just plural.

C.why: You made the owner singular, but the passage describes many thousands of weavers working in their own homes. Several owners ending in s take s'.

D.why: You got "weavers'" right but also added an apostrophe to "loom's." That noun owns nothing and comes right before the plural verb "were."
